claim: ZDBF2 is a paternally expressed imprinted gene located on human chromosome 2q37.1.
source: Zinc finger DBF-type containing 2 (ZDBF2), a paternally expressed gene located on human chromosome 2q37.1, has been reported to regulate neonatal feeding behavior and growth in mice, although its molecular function remains unknown (Kobayashi et al., 2009; Glaser et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Kobayashi et al., 2009; Glaser et al., 2022).

claim: ZDBF2 regulates neonatal feeding behavior and growth in mice.
source: Zinc finger DBF-type containing 2 (ZDBF2), a paternally expressed gene located on human chromosome 2q37.1, has been reported to regulate neonatal feeding behavior and growth in mice, although its molecular function remains unknown (Kobayashi et al., 2009; Glaser et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Kobayashi et al., 2009; Glaser et al., 2022).

claim: The molecular function of ZDBF2 remains unknown.
source: Zinc finger DBF-type containing 2 (ZDBF2), a paternally expressed gene located on human chromosome 2q37.1, has been reported to regulate neonatal feeding behavior and growth in mice, although its molecular function remains unknown (Kobayashi et al., 2009; Glaser et al., 2022).
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text.

claim: There are at least three imprinted genes around the ZDBF2 locus: ZDBF2, GPR1 (alternatively named CMKLR1), and ADAM23.
source: There are at least three imprinted genes, ZDBF2, GPR1 (alternatively named CMKLR1), and ADAM23 around this locus (Hiura et al., 2010; Morcos et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Hiura et al., 2010; Morcos et al., 2011).

claim: The Zdbf2 gene is paternally expressed in the rat.
source: Recently, the Zdbf2 gene was also shown to be paternally expressed in the rat, another member of the Muridae family (Richard Albert et al., 2023; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to a recent study (Richard Albert et al., 2023) and supplementary data.

claim: ZDBF2 imprinting is regulated by two types of imprinted DMRs: a germline DMR located in the intron of the GPR1 gene and a somatic (secondary) imprinted DMR upstream of ZDBF2.
source: Studies have shown that ZDBF2 imprinting is regulated by two types of imprinted DMRs: a germline DMR located in the intron of the GPR1 gene and a somatic (secondary) imprinted DMR upstream of ZDBF2 (Kobayashi et al., 2012b; Kobayashi et al., 2013; Duffié et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Kobayashi et al., 2012b; Kobayashi et al., 2013; Duffié et al., 2014).

claim: The germline DMR at the ZDBF2 locus is methylated on the maternal allele.
source: The germline DMR is methylated on the maternal allele, leading to silencing of GPR1 antisense RNA (GPR1-AS, alternatively named CMKLR1-AS) expression on that allele.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text describing the mechanism of ZDBF2 imprinting.

claim: The paternal allele of the germline DMR is hypomethylated, allowing for the expression of GPR1-AS.
source: In contrast, the paternal allele is hypomethylated, allowing for the expression of GPR1-AS, which is transcribed in the reverse direction of GPR1 (in the same direction as ZDBF2) from the germline DMR.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text describing the mechanism of ZDBF2 imprinting.

claim: GPR1-AS is transcribed in the reverse direction of GPR1 (in the same direction as ZDBF2) from the germline DMR.
source: In contrast, the paternal allele is hypomethylated, allowing for the expression of GPR1-AS, which is transcribed in the reverse direction of GPR1 (in the same direction as ZDBF2) from the germline DMR.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text describing the mechanism of ZDBF2 imprinting.

claim: A fusion transcript of Gpr1-as (Platr12) and Zdbf2 (alternatively named Zdbf2linc or Liz; a long isoform of Zdbf2) has been identified in mice.
source: Although it is not known whether GPR1-AS encodes a protein, a fusion transcript of Gpr1-as (Platr12) and Zdbf2 (alternatively named Zdbf2linc or Liz; a long isoform of Zdbf2) has been identified in mice (Kobayashi et al., 2012b; Duffié et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Kobayashi et al., 2012b; Duffié et al., 2014).

claim: It is not known whether GPR1-AS encodes a protein.
source: Although it is not known whether GPR1-AS encodes a protein, a fusion transcript of Gpr1-as (Platr12) and Zdbf2 (alternatively named Zdbf2linc or Liz; a long isoform of Zdbf2) has been identified in mice (Kobayashi et al., 2012b; Duffié et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text.

claim: The fusion transcript of Gpr1-as and Zdbf2 exhibited an imprinted expression pattern similar to that of human GPR1-AS.
source: Notably, this fusion transcript exhibited an imprinted expression pattern similar to that of human GPR1-AS (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to supplementary data.

claim: Liz transcription counteracts the H3K27me3-mediated repression of Zdbf2 by promoting the deposition of antagonistic DNA methylation at the secondary DMR.
source: Liz transcription counteracts the H3K27me3-mediated repression of Zdbf2 by promoting the deposition of antagonistic DNA methylation at the secondary DMR (Greenberg et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study (Greenberg et al., 2017).

claim: Differential methylation of the germline DMR at the ZDBF2 locus is no longer maintained after implantation because the paternally derived allele also becomes methylated after implantation.
source: Germline DMRs that function as ICRs generally maintain uniparental methylation throughout development; however, differential methylation of the germline DMR is no longer maintained at this locus after implantation because the paternally derived allele also becomes methylated after implantation.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text describing the unique regulatory mechanism at the ZDBF2 locus.

claim: The secondary DMR, rather than germline DMR, maintains the imprinted status of the ZDBF2 locus in somatic cell lineages.
source: Thus, the secondary DMR, rather than germline DMR, is thought to maintain the imprinted status of this locus in somatic cell lineages.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as an inference from the observation that the germline DMR loses differential methylation after implantation.

claim: The unique regulatory mechanism responsible for imprinting at the ZDBF2 locus appears to be conserved between humans and mice.
source: The unique regulatory mechanism responsible for imprinting at the ZDBF2 locus appears to be conserved between humans and mice; however, whether this conservation extends to other mammals remains unexplored.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text based on previous studies.

claim: The first exon of human GPR1-AS overlaps with a MER21C long terminal repeat (LTR).
source: Here, we investigate the evolutionary origin of this mechanism, and show that the first exon of human GPR1-AS overlaps with a MER21C long terminal repeat (LTR), a retrotransposon subfamily specific to Boreoeutherian mammals.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the abstract as a finding of this study.

claim: MER21C is a retrotransposon subfamily specific to Boreoeutherian mammals.
source: Here, we investigate the evolutionary origin of this mechanism, and show that the first exon of human GPR1-AS overlaps with a MER21C long terminal repeat (LTR), a retrotransposon subfamily specific to Boreoeutherian mammals.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the abstract as a finding of this study.

claim: The MER21C insertion occurred in the common ancestor of Euarchontoglires, including primates, rodents, and rabbits.
source: Comparative analyses revealed that this MER21C insertion occurred in the common ancestor of Euarchontoglires, including primates, rodents, and rabbits.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the abstract as a finding of this study based on comparative analyses.

claim: The first exon of mouse Liz displays conserved features with the MER21C-overlapping exon in humans, although not annotated.
source: Although not annotated, the first exon of mouse Liz displays conserved features with the MER21C-overlapping exon in humans.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the abstract as a finding of this study.

claim: GPR1-AS orthologs with LTR-embedded first exons were identified in rabbit and nonhuman primate placentas.
source: In rabbit and nonhuman primate placentas, GPR1-AS orthologs with LTR-embedded first exons were also identified.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the abstract as a finding of this study.

claim: In non-Euarchontoglire mammals such as cow and tammar wallaby, ZDBF2 is biallelically expressed.
source: In contrast, in non-Euarchontoglire mammals such as cow and tammar wallaby, ZDBF2 is biallelically expressed, suggesting absence of imprinting.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the abstract as a finding of this study.

claim: ZDBF2 imprinting emerged in Euarchontoglires via MER21C insertion.
source: These findings suggest that ZDBF2 imprinting emerged in Euarchontoglires via MER21C insertion.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the abstract as a conclusion from the findings.

claim: Post-fertilization activation of retrotransposons can drive lineage-specific acquisition of imprinting.
source: Together with our prior work on LTR-driven imprinting in oocytes, our findings demonstrate that post-fertilization activation of retrotransposons can also drive lineage-specific acquisition of imprinting.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the abstract as a conclusion from the findings.

claim: Genomic imprinting refers to the differential expression of imprinted genes depending on their parental origin.
source: Genomic imprinting is a well-established biological phenomenon that refers to the differential expression of imprinted genes depending on their parental origin (Tucci et al., 2019; Kobayashi, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Tucci et al., 2019; Kobayashi, 2021).

claim: Epigenetic mechanisms, including DNA methylation, histone modification, and noncoding RNA molecules, regulate genomic imprinting.
source: Epigenetic mechanisms, including DNA methylation, histone modification, and noncoding RNA molecules, regulate this process, establishing and maintaining parent-of-origin-specific gene expression patterns.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as established knowledge.

claim: Imprinted genes play vital roles in various biological processes such as fetal growth and development, placental function, metabolism, and behavior.
source: Imprinted genes play vital roles in various biological processes such as fetal growth and development, placental function, metabolism, and behavior.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as established knowledge.

claim: Imprinted genes are often clustered within imprinted domains and regulated by epigenetic marks in specific imprinting control regions (ICRs).
source: These imprinted genes are often clustered within imprinted domains and regulated by epigenetic marks in specific imprinting control regions (ICRs).
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as established knowledge.

claim: The inheritance of parent-of-origin-specific DNA methylation marks from the oocyte or sperm occurs in germline differentially methylated regions (germline DMRs).
source: The inheritance of parent-of-origin-specific DNA methylation marks from the oocyte or sperm occurs in germline differentially methylated regions (germline DMRs), which are propagated in all somatic tissues of the next generation and function as ICRs (therefore, referred to as canonical imprinting).
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as established knowledge.

claim: Germline DMRs are propagated in all somatic tissues of the next generation and function as ICRs.
source: The inheritance of parent-of-origin-specific DNA methylation marks from the oocyte or sperm occurs in germline differentially methylated regions (germline DMRs), which are propagated in all somatic tissues of the next generation and function as ICRs (therefore, referred to as canonical imprinting).
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as established knowledge.

claim: Imprinting patterns can vary significantly among species.
source: Imprinting patterns can vary significantly among species.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as established knowledge.

claim: Nearly 200 imprinted genes have been identified in mice and humans.
source: For example, nearly 200 imprinted genes have been identified in mice and humans.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as established knowledge.

claim: Fewer than half of the imprinted genes identified in mice and humans are imprinted in both species.
source: However, one comparative analysis suggested that fewer than half of these genes are imprinted in both species, suggesting the existence of many species- or lineage-specific imprinted genes (Tucci et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study (Tucci et al., 2019).

claim: The establishment of species-specific imprinting at specific loci can be driven by various evolutionary events, including retrotransposition of genes or transposable elements.
source: The establishment of species-specific imprinting at specific loci can be driven by various evolutionary events, including retrotransposition of genes or transposable elements, which may lead to the acquisition of new genes as imprinted genes or the formation of germline DMRs at CpG-rich regions (CpG islands)(Kobayashi, 2021; Kaneko-Ishino and Ishino, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Kobayashi, 2021; Kaneko-Ishino and Ishino, 2022).

claim: CpG islands may become germline DMRs in the female germline as a consequence of transcription across the CpG island.
source: These CpG islands, often conserved as orthologous sequences across species, may become germline DMRs in the female germline as a consequence of transcription across the CpG island (Chotalia et al., 2009; Kobayashi et al., 2012a).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Chotalia et al., 2009; Kobayashi et al., 2012a).

claim: Transcription across CpG islands may be initiated within transposable elements which have integrated nearby.
source: Such transcription may be initiated within transposable elements which have integrated nearby.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as a mechanism for the establishment of germline DMRs.

claim: Oocyte-specific transcription from upstream promoters, such as integrated LTR retrotransposons, likely played a critical role in the establishment of lineage-specific maternal germline DMRs.
source: Indeed, our previous studies have shown that oocyte-specific transcription from upstream promoters, such as integrated LTR retrotransposons, likely played a critical role in the establishment of lineage-specific maternal germline DMRs (Brind'Amour et al., 2018; Bogutz et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Brind'Amour et al., 2018; Bogutz et al., 2019).

claim: An alternative form of imprinting involves the Polycomb marks H3K27me3 and H2AK119ub1, initially deposited in oocytes.
source: An alternative form of imprinting involves the Polycomb marks H3K27me3 and H2AK119ub1, initially deposited in oocytes (Mei et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study (Mei et al., 2021).

claim: Non-canonical imprints are maternally inherited and silence associated genes during preimplantation.
source: Originally described in rodents, such 'non-canonical' imprints are maternally inherited and in turn silence associated genes during preimplantation.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as established knowledge.

claim: Polycomb marks are converted into DNA methylation over LTR elements, thus maintaining silencing of maternal alleles in the extraembryonic lineage.
source: Subsequently, these Polycomb marks are converted into DNA methylation over LTR elements, thus maintaining silencing of maternal alleles in the extraembryonic lineage (Hanna et al., 2019; Richard Albert et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Hanna et al., 2019; Richard Albert et al., 2023).

claim: ZFP57 and ZNF445 cooperatively maintain ICR methylation, with ZNF445 being more dominant in humans and ZFP57 in mice.
source: In addition, interspecies differences in the regulators of ICRs, such as ZFP57 and ZNF445, as well as species-specific orthologs of DNA methyltransferases, including DNMT3C, are potential species-specific features: ZFP57 and ZNF445 cooperatively maintain ICR methylation, with ZNF445 being more dominant in humans and ZFP57 in mice; and DNMT3C is crucial for a paternally methylated DMR and appears to be specific to Muroidea.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as established knowledge.

claim: DNMT3C is crucial for a paternally methylated DMR and appears to be specific to Muroidea.
source: In addition, interspecies differences in the regulators of ICRs, such as ZFP57 and ZNF445, as well as species-specific orthologs of DNA methyltransferases, including DNMT3C, are potential species-specific features: ZFP57 and ZNF445 cooperatively maintain ICR methylation, with ZNF445 being more dominant in humans and ZFP57 in mice; and DNMT3C is crucial for a paternally methylated DMR and appears to be specific to Muroidea.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as established knowledge.

claim: Interspecies differences in the regulators of ICRs might have contributed to the establishment of species-specific imprinted genes.
source: These features might also have contributed to the establishment of species-specific imprinted genes (Barau et al., 2016; Takahashi et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Barau et al., 2016; Takahashi et al., 2019).

claim: Public human tissue RNA-seq data sets show that GPR1-AS transcription is detectable in the placenta at a relatively low level (RPKM value of around 0.45–1.8).
source: Public human tissue RNA-seq data sets show that GPR1-AS transcription is detectable in the placenta, albeit at a relatively low level (RPKM value of around 0.45–1.8), but is significantly suppressed in other tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Fagerberg et al., 2014; Duff et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and citations to previous studies (Fagerberg et al., 2014; Duff et al., 2015).

claim: GPR1-AS transcription is significantly suppressed in human tissues other than the placenta.
source: Public human tissue RNA-seq data sets show that GPR1-AS transcription is detectable in the placenta, albeit at a relatively low level (RPKM value of around 0.45–1.8), but is significantly suppressed in other tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Fagerberg et al., 2014; Duff et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and citations to previous studies (Fagerberg et al., 2014; Duff et al., 2015).

claim: Conventional non-directional RNA-seq datasets may not be sufficient to accurately detect GPR1-AS in different species.
source: This suggests that conventional RNA-seq datasets may not be sufficient to accurately detect GPR1-AS in different species.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as an inference from the observation that GPR1-AS was not detected in mouse placental data using conventional RNA-seq.

claim: GPR1-AS transcripts can be identified in placental tissues using deep directional RNA-seq data.
source: Thus, GPR1-AS transcripts can be identified in placental tissues using deep directional RNA-seq data.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as a conclusion from the analysis of directional RNA-seq data.

claim: GPR1-AS orthologs were identified in chimpanzees and rabbits but were not observed in cows, pigs, or opossums.
source: Among these datasets, GPR1-AS orthologs were identified in chimpanzees and rabbits but were not observed in cows, pigs, or opossums (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2 showing the results of transcript prediction analysis.

claim: Rabbit GPR1-AS is expressed only in placental lineages.
source: Additionally, we performed directional RNA-seq of tissues from the embryonic proper (embryonic disc: ED) of multiple individual animal embryos but did not identify any GPR1-AS-like transcripts in any of these samples (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). Thus, rabbit GPR1-AS is expressed only in placental lineages.
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing the absence of GPR1-AS in embryonic proper tissues.

claim: The regulatory region driving GPR1-AS transcripts likely originated in the common ancestor of the Euarchontoglires group.
source: Identification of GPR1-AS in several primate species as well as mice and rabbits but not in cows, pigs, or opossums indicates that the regulatory region driving GPR1-AS transcripts likely originated in the common ancestor of the Euarchontoglires group.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as an inference from the distribution of GPR1-AS orthologs across species.

claim: ZDBF2 is expressed from both alleles in all bovine and wallaby tissues analyzed.
source: We identified available SNPs at the 3'-UTR of ZDBF2 in each of these mammals, and Sanger-sequencing-based polymorphism analysis showed the expression of both ZDBF2 alleles in all bovine and wallaby tissues analyzed (Figure 3A–B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 3A–B and Supplementary file 1 showing the results of allele-specific expression analysis.

claim: Paternal allele-specific expression of ZDBF2 was observed in rhesus macaques and rabbits.
source: Similar analyses were performed using blood samples from rhesus macaques and rabbits, in which GPR1-AS was identified. Consistent with our findings in humans and mice, we observed paternal allele-specific expression of ZDBF2 in these species (Figure 3C–D), in clear contrast to the bi-allelic expression observed in the embryonic, fetal, and adult tissues of tammar wallabies and cattle.
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 3C–D showing the results of allele-specific expression analysis.

claim: Analysis of published whole-genome bisulfite sequencing data from rhesus macaque oocytes and sperm revealed an oocyte-methylated germline DMR at the first exon of GPR1-AS.
source: Analysis of published whole-genome bisulfite sequencing data from rhesus macaque oocytes and sperm revealed DMRs between both germ cells, including an oocyte-methylated germline DMR at the first exon of GPR1-AS (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Gao et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and citation to a previous study (Gao et al., 2017).

claim: Analysis of published whole-genome bisulfite sequencing data for porcine and bovine oocytes and sperm showed no oocyte-methylated germline DMRs in the GPR1 intragenic region.
source: In contrast, analysis of published whole-genome bisulfite sequencing data for porcine and bovine oocytes and sperm (Ivanova et al., 2020) showed no oocyte-methylated germline DMRs in the GPR1 intragenic region, where GPR1-AS is transcribed from an intron of GPR1 in humans and rhesus macaques (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and citation to a previous study (Ivanova et al., 2020).

claim: ZDBF2 imprinting is restricted to mammals within the Euarchontoglires group.
source: Taken together, these results support the hypothesis that ZDBF2 imprinting is restricted to mammals within the Euarchontoglires group.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as a conclusion from the findings.

claim: The first exon of all GPR1-AS orthologs, except for mouse Liz, overlapped with an annotated MER21C element.
source: Notably, the first exon of all GPR1-AS orthologs, except for mouse Liz, overlapped with an annotated MER21C element, a member of the LTR retrotransposon subfamily (Figures 1 and 2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figures 1 and 2, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C showing the overlap of GPR1-AS first exons with MER21C elements.

claim: MER21C retrotransposons are broadly present in Boroeutherians.
source: While MER21C retrotransposons are broadly present in Boroeutherians, among the mammals tested, only primate and rabbit genomes have MER21C in the GPR1 intron, where the first exon of GPR1-AS is located.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as an observation from the comparative analysis.

claim: Among the mammals tested, only primate and rabbit genomes have MER21C in the GPR1 intron, where the first exon of GPR1-AS is located.
source: While MER21C retrotransposons are broadly present in Boroeutherians, among the mammals tested, only primate and rabbit genomes have MER21C in the GPR1 intron, where the first exon of GPR1-AS is located.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as an observation from the comparative analysis.

claim: MER21C (or MER21B retrotransposons that showed high similarity to MER21C) was found inserted in the introns of GPR1 in five groups of Euarchontoglires, including primates, colugos, treeshrews, rabbits, and rodents, with the exception of mouse, rat, and hamster.
source: Among eutherians, we found the insertion of MER21C (or MER21B retrotransposons that showed high similarity to MER21C) in the introns of GPR1 in five groups of Euarchontoglires, including primates, colugos, treeshrews, rabbits, and rodents, with the exception of mouse, rat, and hamster (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 4 showing the comparative analysis of LTR sequence locations.

claim: Reanalysis of mouse, rat, and hamster genomes using less stringent RepeatMasker parameters failed to reveal the presence of an MER21C insertion in the relevant regions.
source: As the default parameters of RepeatMasker may not detect degenerate LTR sequences, we reanalyzed these three rodent species using less stringent RepeatMasker parameters but again failed to reveal the presence of an MER21C insertion in the relevant regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing the results of the reanalysis.

claim: Multiple genome alignments from UCSC/Cactus track indicated that the MER21C-derived sequence on the human GPR1-AS is likely conserved in mammals belonging to Euarchontoglires, including mouse, rat, and hamster.
source: However, multiple genome alignments from UCSC/Cactus track indicated that the MER21C-derived sequence on the human GPR1-AS is likely conserved in mammals belonging to Euarchontoglires, including mouse, rat, and hamster (Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Armstrong et al., 2020; Zoonomia Consortium, 2020), albeit with a high level of degeneracy in the latter.
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and citations to previous studies (Armstrong et al., 2020; Zoonomia Consortium, 2020).

claim: Pairwise alignment revealed high identities between primate sequences (identity: 71–72%) and the consensus MER21C sequence compared to rabbit (60%) and mouse sequences (46%).
source: Pairwise alignment revealed high identities between primate sequences (identity: 71–72%) and the consensus MER21C sequence compared to rabbit (60%) and mouse sequences (46%) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1A showing the results of pairwise alignment.

claim: The sequence identity of the first exon of mouse Liz to the consensus MER21C sequence is so low that it cannot be distinguished from other LTRs or retrotransposons.
source: The sequence identity in mice is so low that it cannot be distinguished from other LTRs or retrotransposons, which explains why it was not classified as MER21C by RepeatMasker analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C showing the results of sequence comparison.

claim: Multiple sequence alignments and phylogenetic tree reconstruction reveal that the rabbit and mouse sequences deviate to a greater extent from the consensus MER21C sequence than the cluster formed by the primate sequences.
source: Multiple sequence alignments and phylogenetic tree reconstruction reveal that the rabbit and mouse sequences deviate to a greater extent from the consensus MER21C sequence than the cluster formed by the primate sequences, indicating that a greater number of mutations have accumulated in the non-primate lineage of Euarchontoglires since their divergence from primates (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 5A showing the phylogenetic tree.

claim: A greater number of mutations have accumulated in the non-primate lineage of Euarchontoglires since their divergence from primates.
source: Multiple sequence alignments and phylogenetic tree reconstruction reveal that the rabbit and mouse sequences deviate to a greater extent from the consensus MER21C sequence than the cluster formed by the primate sequences, indicating that a greater number of mutations have accumulated in the non-primate lineage of Euarchontoglires since their divergence from primates (Figure 5A).
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as an inference from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The observation that a greater number of mutations have accumulated in the non-primate lineage of Euarchontoglires aligns with the shorter generation time of lagomorphs and rodents compared to primates.
source: This observation aligns with the shorter generation time of lagomorphs and rodents compared to primates (Wu and Li, 1985; Huttley et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Wu and Li, 1985; Huttley et al., 2007).

claim: The first exon of mouse Liz exhibits promoter activity greater than that of the human GPR1-AS promoter in HEK293T cells.
source: Strikingly, the first exon of mouse Liz exhibits promoter activity greater than that of the human GPR1-AS promoter, despite the relatively low sequence similarity between the Liz first exon and the consensus MER21C sequence (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 2 showing the results of the dual reporter assay.

claim: Despite substantial sequence divergence, the functional elements responsible for initiating transcription of Liz in the mouse are derived from the same MER21C relic annotated in the human locus and can drive robust expression in human cells.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that despite substantial sequence divergence, the functional elements responsible for initiating transcription of Liz in the mouse are derived from the same MER21C relic annotated in the human locus and can drive robust expression in human cells.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as a conclusion from the dual reporter assay results.

claim: A common region containing an ETS family transcription factor (ELF1 and ELF2) binding site was found in the MER21C-derived sequences.
source: Through this analysis, we found a common region that contained an ETS family transcription factor (ELF1 and ELF2) binding site, which had significant matches with E-values <0.01 and q-values <0.01 (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 5B and C showing the results of the motif analysis.

claim: TFAP2 and ZSCAN4 binding motifs were identified at the first exon of human GPR1-AS and mouse Liz, respectively.
source: Additionally, we identified the TFAP2 and ZSCAN4 binding motifs (with p-values = 1.58×10–5 and 7.24×10–7) from the JASPAR database at the first exon of human GPR1-AS and mouse Liz, respectively (Figure 5B and D).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 5B and D showing the results of the motif analysis.

claim: TFAP2C and ZSCAN4C are activated in the placental lineage and preimplantation embryos, respectively.
source: Since TFAP2C and ZSCAN4C are activated in the placental lineage and preimplantation embryos, respectively (Zhang et al., 2019; Papuchova and Latos, 2022; Figure 5—figure supplement 3), binding of these transcription factors may play a role in the transcriptional activation of GPR1-AS or Liz during embryogenesis, and in turn imprinting of ZDBF2.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Zhang et al., 2019; Papuchova and Latos, 2022) and reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Binding of TFAP2C and ZSCAN4C may play a role in the transcriptional activation of GPR1-AS or Liz during embryogenesis, and in turn imprinting of ZDBF2.
source: Since TFAP2C and ZSCAN4C are activated in the placental lineage and preimplantation embryos, respectively (Zhang et al., 2019; Papuchova and Latos, 2022; Figure 5—figure supplement 3), binding of these transcription factors may play a role in the transcriptional activation of GPR1-AS or Liz during embryogenesis, and in turn imprinting of ZDBF2.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as a speculation based on the expression patterns of TFAP2C and ZSCAN4C.

claim: GPR1-AS is reported to be expressed only briefly during embryogenesis, both before and after implantation, with the exception of the placental lineage.
source: GPR1-AS is reported to be expressed only briefly during embryogenesis, both before and after implantation, with the exception of the placental lineage.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as established knowledge.

claim: Human GPR1-AS has been identified in ES cells.
source: For instance, human GPR1-AS has been identified in ES cells, and mouse Liz expression has been observed in blastocyst-to-gastrulation embryos but not in gametes (Kobayashi et al., 2012b; Kobayashi et al., 2013; Duffié et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Kobayashi et al., 2012b; Kobayashi et al., 2013; Duffié et al., 2014).

claim: GPR1-AS was only detected at the 8 cell stage, ICM, and TE in human embryos.
source: Among the datasets from oocytes; zygotes; 2-, 4-, and 8 cell embryos; inner cell mass (ICM); and TE from blastocysts, GPR1-AS was only detected at the 8 cell stage, ICM, and TE; GPR-AS-like transcripts were detected as predicted transcripts, with TPM values above 1 (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 6 showing the results of expression analysis.

claim: GPR1-AS expression likely begins at the 8 cell stage in humans.
source: This indicates that GPR1-AS expression likely begins at the 8 cell stage in humans.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as an inference from the observation that GPR1-AS was detected at the 8 cell stage but not at earlier stages.

claim: At the GPR1-ZDBF2 locus, both GPR1 and ZDBF2 were expressed in oocytes, but only GPR1 was downregulated following fertilization and became undetectable beyond the 8 cell stage.
source: However, at the GPR1-ZDBF2 locus, both GPR1 and ZDBF2 were expressed in oocytes, but only GPR1 was downregulated following fertilization and became undetectable beyond the 8 cell stage (Figure 6 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 6 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3 showing the expression patterns.

claim: MER21C expression increased from the 4-cell to 8-cell stage and peaked at the TE in human embryos.
source: We also examined MER21C expression at each stage and found that it increased from the 4-cell to 8-cell stage and peaked at the TE, coinciding with the appearance of GPR1-AS (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1 showing the expression patterns.

claim: ZNF789 is a key KRAB-ZFP that binds MER21C.
source: Moreover, focusing on Kruppel-associated box zinc-finger proteins (KRAB-ZFPs) involved in the suppression of transposable elements, we observed that ZNF789—a key KRAB-ZFP that binds MER21C—was specifically downregulated at the 4 cell stage (Figure 5—figure supplement 3; Imbeault et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study (Imbeault et al., 2017) and reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: ZNF789 was specifically downregulated at the 4 cell stage in human embryos.
source: Moreover, focusing on Kruppel-associated box zinc-finger proteins (KRAB-ZFPs) involved in the suppression of transposable elements, we observed that ZNF789—a key KRAB-ZFP that binds MER21C—was specifically downregulated at the 4 cell stage (Figure 5—figure supplement 3; Imbeault et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 3 showing the expression patterns.

claim: GPR1-AS expression begins in the preimplantation embryo, concurrently with a transcription factor/repressor milieu permissive for expression from its MER21C-derived promoter.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that GPR1-AS expression begins in the preimplantation embryo, concurrently with a transcription factor/repressor milieu permissive for expression from its MER21C-derived promoter.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as a conclusion from the findings.

claim: Both sequences that constitute the oocyte-derived germline DMR exhibit an enrichment of H3K4me3 in sperm or male germ cells.
source: Both sequences that constitute the oocyte-derived germline DMR exhibit an enrichment of H3K4me3 in sperm or male germ cells, consistent with DNA hypomethylation in sperm.

claim: The sequences that constitute the oocyte-derived germline DMR show an enrichment of H3K27ac in pluripotent stem cells (such as ES and iPS cells).
source: These sequences also show an enrichment of H3K27ac in pluripotent stem cells (such as ES and iPS cells).
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as an observation from the ChIP-Atlas database analysis.

claim: The first exon of mouse Liz is enriched for H3K9me3, a repressive mark which is deposited at retrotransposons, in multiple cell types and tissues.
source: Although, as discussed above, the first exon of mouse Liz has not been computationally determined as an LTR (according to the RepBase database), the mouse sequence is also enriched for H3K9me3, a repressive mark which is deposited at retrotransposons, in multiple cell types and tissues.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as an observation from the ChIP-Atlas database analysis.

claim: Human and mouse germline DMRs coincided with the TFAP2C peak (trophoblast stem cells) and ZSCAN4C peak (ES cells), respectively.

claim: The specific regulatory pathways governing the activation of GPR1-AS and Liz may differ between species, perhaps reflected in differences in the specific set of transcription factors involved.

evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as a speculation based on the differences in transcription factor binding motifs.

claim: ZDBF2 does not directly influence cell differentiation or ontogeny, such as embryogenesis, but rather affects individual growth through an indirect pathway involving feeding behavior.
source: ZDBF2 does not directly influence cell differentiation or ontogeny, such as embryogenesis, but rather affects individual growth through an indirect pathway involving feeding behavior.

claim: The insertion of MER21C LTR at the GPR1 intragenic region in the common ancestor of Euarchontoglires was the crucial event in the genesis of imprinting of the ZDBF2 gene.
source: We propose that the first exon of GPR1-AS is derived from a MER21C retrotransposon and that the insertion of this LTR at the GPR1 intragenic region in the common ancestor of Euarchontoglires was the crucial event in the genesis of imprinting of the ZDBF2 gene (Figure 7).

claim: Two paternally expressed imprinted genes, PEG10/SIRH1, and PEG11/RTL1/SIRH2, that encode GAG-POL proteins of sushi-ichi LTR retrotransposons have been identified in mammals and are essential for placenta formation and maintenance.
source: Two paternally expressed imprinted genes, PEG10/SIRH1, and PEG11/RTL1/SIRH2, that encode GAG-POL proteins of sushi-ichi LTR retrotransposons have been identified in mammals and are essential for placenta formation and maintenance (Kaneko-Ishino and Ishino, 2012).

claim: The presence of PEG10/SIRH1 and PEG11/RTL1/SIRH2 provides evidence that LTR insertions have played a significant role in genomic imprinting as well as placentation throughout evolution of placental mammals.
source: The presence of these genes provides evidence that LTR insertions have played a significant role in genomic imprinting as well as placentation throughout evolution of placental mammals.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as an inference from the existence of PEG10/SIRH1 and PEG11/RTL1/SIRH2.

claim: The ZDBF2 gene is present in all vertebrate genomes.
source: In contrast, while the ZDBF2 gene is present in all vertebrate genomes, it is only imprinted in mammals belonging to the Euarchontoglires superorder of placental mammals.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as an observation about the distribution of ZDBF2.

claim: ZDBF2 is only imprinted in mammals belonging to the Euarchontoglires superorder of placental mammals.
source: In contrast, while the ZDBF2 gene is present in all vertebrate genomes, it is only imprinted in mammals belonging to the Euarchontoglires superorder of placental mammals.
evidence: Stated explicitly in the text as a finding of this study.

claim: LTRs that act as alternative promoters produce unique transcripts in the oocyte, referred to as LITs (LTR-initiated transcripts).

claim: The key difference between LTRs that drive LITs in oocytes and the LTR retrotransposon focused on in this study is the stage in development when LTR (re)activation occurs, i.e., before or after fertilization, respectively.
